body:
## Problem Statement

A sync halted by a restack conflict has one supported exit: `an continue`. Of the forty commands in `an --help`,
`continue` is the only recovery verb; there is no `abort`, `cancel` or `skip`. The two matches for "abort" in the
help text are prose about `git rebase --abort`, not a command.

That becomes a trap when the right resolution is "this branch is obsolete". Observed on 0.6.13, syncing a
seven-branch stack plus three unrelated local-only branches:

```
Hit conflict restacking storybook-docs-button-base on main.
...
To fix and continue your previous Anthracite command:
(1) resolve the listed merge conflicts
(2) mark them as resolved with an add .
(3) run an continue to continue executing your previous Anthracite command
an rebase --abort only cancels the active rebase; it does not undo earlier completed operations or restore all
parent relationships.
```

The conflicting branch was a four-month-old prototype whose code the trunk had since superseded; it conflicted
precisely because trunk now imports from a package what the branch adds locally. There was nothing to resolve. So
the branch was deleted — and then:

```
$ an continue
ERROR: No matching owned active sync rebase; completed work may remain after abort or publication failure.
Sync recovery preserved. ... No unverified queue or automatic rollback is permitted.

$ an ls
ERROR: Finish the pending sync before starting another operation. Sync recovery preserved. Inspect git status,
git log, source refs and saved .gtcontinue in the original project.
```

The only way out was to read the 64 KB `.git/.gtcontinue`, confirm by hand that `trunkCompleted`,
`cleanupCompleted` and `completedMaintenance` accounted for everything the record was tracking, and delete the
file. That is archaeology, not a workflow — and the message that names the file also says that touching it is not
permitted.

Three things compound it. The failure message names `git rebase --abort` without saying that running it ends the
only supported recovery path. The pending-sync gate refuses read-only commands, so the message that says
"inspect" disables `an ls`, the best tool for inspecting. And deleting the obsolete branch — the correct
resolution — is itself the action that strands the sync, because `continue` looks only for an active rebase rather
than at the record it already holds.

## Solution

Give a halted sync a way to be abandoned, and make the state it leaves behind legible.

`an sync --abort` discards the saved record after reporting what was already applied, what will stay un-done, and
which branches still need maintenance. It performs no merge, push or PR edit, and it does not reset trunk or
overwrite feature heads; it ends an operation rather than undoing one. Where manual deletion of `.gtcontinue`
remains the fallback, the refusal says so instead of warning the reader off it.

Continuation also reads the record rather than only the rebase. A pending participant whose branch no longer
exists is nothing left to do for that branch, so `continue` reports it and proceeds to the remaining ones. The
record carries the trunk target, the node list and the completed sets, which is enough to resume without the
rebase that was aborted.

Read-only commands stay available while a sync is pending. `ls`, `log`, `info`, `children` and `pr` change no
state, and the recovery guidance asks the user to inspect.

Finally, a conflict on a branch Anthracite has already reported as local-only can name the cheaper answer. Two
lines above the conflict it printed `storybook-docs-button-base is local-only; remote refresh skipped (no pull
request)`. Saying "this branch has no pull request; if it is obsolete, `an delete <branch>` and run sync again"
would have replaced the whole detour, with a command that already exists.

Keep the existing protections: no automatic rollback, no silent feature overwrite, no trunk reset, and the frozen,
dirty-file and worktree guards.

## User Stories

1. As a developer, I want to abandon a halted sync, so that concluding a branch is obsolete does not leave the
   repository in a state no command can clear.
2. As a developer, I want the abort to tell me what was applied and what stays un-done, so that I know the state I
   am left in without reading a saved record.
3. As a developer, I want `an continue` to skip a pending branch that no longer exists and carry on with the rest,
   so that deleting an obsolete branch is a resolution rather than a dead end.
4. As a developer, I want `an ls` and the other read-only commands to work while a sync is pending, so that the
   guidance to inspect is possible to follow.
5. As a developer, I want the failure message to say that `git rebase --abort` ends the supported recovery path,
   so that I do not take it without knowing the cost.
6. As a developer, I want the refusal to name the way out rather than only the saved file, so that manual deletion
   is either sanctioned or unnecessary.
7. As a developer, I want a conflict on a branch with no pull request to mention `an delete`, so that the cheapest
   resolution is offered where it applies.
8. As an agent, I want abandoning a sync to be a single command with a reported outcome, so that unattended
   recovery does not depend on inspecting a private file.
9. As a maintainer, I want the existing rollback, overwrite, trunk-reset and frozen protections preserved, so that
   an exit from a halted sync is not an exit from its safeguards.

title: Give a halted sync a way out other than an continue
